176.t: Meeting Bunk Johnson in Lake Charles
176.s: De De says he met Bunk Johnson years later in Lake Charles with a drummer named Foster; Bunk had false teeth but still played strongly.
176.q: At the time he was playing with, well, I know one of them then. That was a brother like Chiney. Chiney, what he was called Chiney with a drummer with Celeste Ant one time.

176.t: The St. Bernard trio and who went to Bunkie
176.s: Billie lists the three-piece group, then the musicians she took to Bunkie, including Kid Ernest and Frank Gibbs.
176.q: Let me see. Who had one drum? Was it Albert Jive? Albert. Right. I had Albert Jive on drums, D on trumpet, I'm on piano, just three pieces.

870.t: Bunk Johnson's generosity and the home he never bought
870.s: Synigal remembers Bunk as a fine, charming player who gave away his money and died before buying a home; the block ends in garbled ASR looping.
870.q: Bunk Jones. Bunk Jones was the father of those guys. He comes to music. So many of them, I can't recall right now exactly that band. He played music with Bunk Jones. He was a fine player. A good mixer. He was very charming, too. He was a fellow who gave his heart out to everybody else and leave…

870.t: Bunk Johnson's early career and travels
870.s: Bunk was playing at 15 or 16, later toured widely and was a professional in New York; Armstrong is said to have played with him.
870.q: Oh, yes. He went to St. Louis with his band. He went to Chicago with his band. He went all of them. He went here with his band. He used to go all around with his band. He didn't use it.

240.t: Was Bunk's late playing representative of his early years?
240.s: The interviewer asks whether Bunk at 68 or 69 showed what he could do earlier; Mike cannot say.
240.ch: Bunk Johnson and the New Orleans scene
240.q: I don't, I don't think that.

240.t: Meeting Bunk Johnson around 1940 and rumors he taught Louis Armstrong
240.s: Mike recalls seeing Bunk play in about 1939-41 shortly before entering the service, and what he heard and read about Bunk teaching Louis.
240.ch: Bunk Johnson and the New Orleans scene
240.q: No, I didn't play Bugs home. Yeah. So, Bugs didn't have any. That's a time that I can recall. So, I was told. I mean, I'm quoting with Paul Barbrain. Yeah.

14.t: Bunk Johnson leaves; Baby Lovett kept home; Bunk in Alexandria in 1908
14.s: Musicians got scared and left on the train, Lovett was fetched back, and Bunk went to Houston; Love dates Bunk in Alexandria to 1908.
14.q: Yeah. Yeah. You see, the man just left. They got scared. Yeah. They got on the train. David Lovett was going to leave there too, but Dr. Brown knew them very well, you know, and went and got him. They got his ticket and everything. That was waiting down and said, you can't run off from home like…

14.t: Bands that played the Red Book and Bunk Johnson's uncle Willie Young
14.s: Love lists the Alexandria bands that played the Red Book and rehearsed together on Sundays, and describes Willie Young, Bunk Johnson's uncle, as a faker.
14.q: Yeah. He played by Bronk Johnson playing the trumpet. And Harry Walker in Alexander. Well, they had some different bands around there. You know, they all played the Red Book. We was all connected together, you see. We had a big orchestra used to rehearse every Sunday. We just rehearsed over to…

237.t: Bunk Johnson sitting in at the Yellow Front
237.s: Lovett says Bunk sat in rather than led, was paid, and did not stay long; Lovett never spent time in New Orleans.
237.ch: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
237.q: That's right. No, I didn't stay in New Orleans very long.

237.t: Why Bunk Johnson passed through Kansas City
237.s: Smith and Lovett say Bunk played at the Yellow Front but did not come to stay or look for work.
237.ch: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
237.q: Well, I don't think he came in to stay, you know, he didn't come to stay. It's hard to get those guys out of New Orleans, man, I'll tell you that.

248.t: Bunk Johnson as a substitute trumpeter
248.s: Dawson says Bunk sat in for others and never led his own band.
248.q: Bunk? Bunk, uh, I played in a band that he played in, but I never did, uh, because he played in, you know, he was a trumpet player that he'd come around and play, say, like, uh, at Fruit Close, at, at, at, at Harry Parker. At, uh, uh, Huntson Nagel, Billy Phillips. He'd come, the fellas would hire…

771.t: Bunk Johnson's reading and soft style in the Superior Band
771.s: Bunk read well, played Joplin rags in slow tempo with a soft touch, and was ruined by drinking after joining the Eagle Band.
771.q: Yeah, Bunk, he would read, yes, he could read, sure. We used to play all that old Joplin music, you know? Frog Legs and Cresanum and all that. We had the Red Book, you saw those books. Yeah, sure, I know. Yeah, we used to play all that, yeah. He read well, yeah.

1027.t: Playing with Bunk Johnson on North Broadway in 1945-46
1027.s: Rinker recalls being asked to sit in with Bunk Johnson, Darnell Howard and Don Ewell at a short North Side engagement, and what Bunk's early New Orleans style meant.
1027.ch: South Side scene and Bunk Johnson
1027.q: and I played a little with him. I can't remember who invited me any longer. Well when Bunk came it was

258.t: Playing with Bunk Johnson in Ike Jenkins's band and hearing Stardust
258.s: In Crowley Thomas drummed for Ike Jenkins, who brought in Bunk Johnson, and first heard Stardust from him; they praise Bunk's musicianship.
258.q: I was in a band in Crowley, Louisiana, called Ike Jenkins Band. And Bunk Johnson, well he lived in New Iberia. Well he, sometime when Ike Jenkins needed a trumpet player, he'd send over to New Iberia and get Bunk Johnson and have Bunk Johnson come to Crowley, Crowley, Louisiana. But Bunk would come…

259.t: Playing like Bunk and Bunk Johnson's travels
259.s: Vincent says Richard played much like Bunk and describes Bunk's wandering to California and Chicago and hard times on tour.
259.q: So he didn't know who bunk was? No, he wasn't playing at that time. He was kind of young, kind of playing. Been playing around about 15 years. And see, bunk left here, good while. Bunk went up here, and knew I buried him a long time. Then he went out to California, Chicago, and different places…

571.t: Bunk's playing in the 1940s versus the 1920s
571.s: George says Bunk played far better before losing his teeth, with more volume, range and execution.
571.ch: Mandeville, Bunk Johnson and society banquets
571.q: Well, he was much better. I know that for a fact, because I played the last jobs with Bunk, and Bunk had his teeth, so I know that for a fact.

734.t: Bunk Johnson's playing and his style
734.s: Bunk played with Gabriel from New Iberia; his style is music, unlike rock and roll; his own reading limits.
734.q: Bunk was living now and yet. Here in New Orleans went out? Yeah, yeah, he went out there. Because Bunk lived out of New Iberia, you know, a long time too. Yeah, yeah, well, he played with Gabriel, uh, when he was in New Iberia, see. He come out and played. We'd spit up our band whenever we'd get…

46.t: Bunk Johnson's disappearance and Esquire concert
46.s: He tells of Bunk's sudden rise, his leaving for a rice farm, and the later concert and New York trip.
46.ch: Hightower: New Orleans parades and early players
46.q: Yeah. They wanted me and I wouldn't even go. Because they had set up. Now they went down there and bought Bunk I think a set of teeth. And wait until he trained himself to them, see.

12.t: Bunk Johnson in New Orleans and in the 1940s comeback
12.s: He heard Bunk as a child and again in 1945; the 1940s band kept the old style, with George Lewis and the Marrero family.
12.q: When I first heard Bunk, I was a kid around nine or ten years old. He was playing with the Superior Band. Maggill was playing with the Imperial. Bunk was the radiest trumpet player at that time in New Orleans, what we call Gut Bucket later on. He was a kid around nine or ten years old. He was a…

836.t: Bunk Johnson's age when he died
836.s: Allen asks how old Bunk Johnson was; Mr. Senegal estimates close to 70 and calls him a fine man.
836.q: Well, Bunk Johnson was, let me see, when Bunk Johnson died, I think Bunk Johnson was about 60 to 80 years old, close to 70, at that time. So he's older than you, huh? He's older than I, yeah. He's about four or five years old. Bunk Johnson was a fine, good age, fine man. She wrote there.

280.t: Playing a concert with Bunk Johnson in Chicago
280.s: Asked about Bunk Johnson and George Lewis, Williams says he played with Bunk, who hung out at his place while in Chicago.
280.ch: Starting out in New Orleans and Chicago
280.q: can't say car no george lewis wasn't in it just bunk your central bunk oh yeah and they had the other band place on here yeah yeah i played with bunk let me see i had saloon i had a cabin at that time bunk hung in my place the whole time he was here oh really my place was to hang out for all…

591.t: Bunk Johnson's comeback after twenty years
591.s: They agree Bunk proved himself by returning after a long layoff.
591.q: And he never come back. Yeah. And I know some that didn't lay off and was shot.

635.t: Bunk Johnson's decline, his rediscovery in 1937 and the horn
635.s: Foster explains how drinking ruined Bunk, how he barely recognized Bunk in 1937, and who bought Bunk his horn.
635.ch: New Orleans bands, players and halls
635.q: He never, all his trouble that Bunk ever got into was himself. Himself. See, just drinking. And Bunk, just didn't start drinking. Bunk was drinking for a long time. Bunk left New Orleans about 1910 and I didn't see Bunk no more until 1937 and I didn't know Bunk. See, I know the Bunk but I didn't…

881.s: He tried to play with Rene's blues in C sharp and played with Bunk in Chicago in the 1940s.
881.ch: Becoming a player; Rene, Bunk and Armstrong
881.q: Well René played in C Sharp. You mean C Sharp. C Sharp. Well that's the same thing. I sat in there with that, I grabbed the trumbo one night, Morrissey here and played with him. And I was feeling around him, you know. You were trying to find the trumbo? Feeling all around, trying to find the key.…

55.t: Bunk Johnson's sweet tone and later career
55.s: Bunk's sweet style, how he imitated Bolden, and how Bill Russell revived him.
55.q: Bunk never was a rough corner player. He never was rock. Bunk always a sweet corner player. A musical player. He played as much corner as he used to drink. I was supposed to lick the head too. Bunk was a nice fella.

637.t: Lazy Daddy Fillmore and Bunk's soft, sweet trumpet
637.s: Brief talk of Lazy Daddy Fillmore, then Bunk's band and his soft, sweet playing compared with Bolden and Keppard.
637.q: Uh-uh. Eddie wasn't about the teeth that much. It wasn't that. Eddie never was no loud trumpet player, you know. He used to play soft and sweet. Low, you know. Yeah. All the way he had his own teeth. He used to clean up all of them for that.

270.s: Sayles never played with Bunk Johnson or George Lewis; he was in Chicago when Bunk was brought back.
270.q: No, no. I never played with the bunk. No. Well, I remember hearing about him those days and everything, but I mean, I was in Chicago when they picked him up and then he took over with George Lewis Band. I was in Chicago.

909.t: Bunk Johnson and E. Vans band at Thibodaux
909.s: Bunk came to get Morris on his last visit but took Jim Robinson; Morris recalls running into Bunk's band out in the country.
909.q: Sure, I used to play with Bunk Oh, yeah When Bunk first come here to leave here that last time, he come here to get me Oh, yeah But I was busy working, that's why he did to take Jim Crow And then Jim Crow and Howard and them, they was working together all the time So he couldn't get me the first…

760.t: Hearing Bunk Johnson in Houston in 1923
760.s: He first hears Bunk Johnson on an advertising wagon in Houston and praises his power and tone as a young man.
760.q: Well, I met Bunk. The first time I ever heard Bunk play was in Houston, Texas. I used to hear him talk about Bunk, but I had never heard him play. So one day we were playing an advertisement in a wagon for a dance. And they were on a wagon playing an advertisement for a show, for a theater. And…

306.t: Bunk Johnson teaching Rene's brother for a bottle of wine
306.s: Rene recalls Bunk Johnson, a wine drinker who gave his brother ideas on trumpet.
306.ch: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
306.q: Oh yeah, I knew Bunk, sure. You know Bunk, sure, my brother plenty of it. And you know what he used to teach him for? A 10 cent bottle of wine. That's all. Did Bunk drink? Yeah, he'd drink wine. He was a wine drinker. He was one of the finest men I ever seen, man. He'd come and cook red beans and…

89.t: Playing "The Entertainer" from the Bunk Johnson album and Bunk's playing
89.s: They play the Bunk arrangement of The Entertainer, which followed original parts, and he describes Bunk using false teeth.
89.ch: Recollections of bands, dances and tours
89.q: arrangement that was made about 1916 or 1917, so it gave it really the authentic sound of just how 'The Entertainer' was played many, many years ago. Most of the numbers that we did on this album Bunk had parts to them, you know, and we adhered right to the part and we played a few solos, but…

18.s: He played a gig and a New Jersey recording with Bunk Johnson, who was old and drunk; they barely talked.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: Well, he's a trumpet player. I played a couple of engagements with him. They sent for him to come to New York and play one gig at the Army Club there on 52nd Street. And I played one, no, we did a recording down in New Jersey; and he's playing behind a crate too loud, pushing him further too loud;…

412.t: The collectors bring Bunk Johnson's band to New York
412.s: The collectors dug Bunk Johnson up, got him teeth and a trumpet and brought him to New York with George Lewis, Jim Robinson and Baby Dodds. Hodes listened every night.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: Just rehearsed and made the date. So into this scene the collectors, especially the Jazz Information, because I like to think of Ralph Gleason and Gene Williams and Rudy Blesh and people like that, began to reach out to do more. And that's how they bought -- they found Bunk Johnson and brought him…
